Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 1–3:

Madaniyya (Medinan), and it has seventy-three verses [it was revealed after Al ʿImran]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

On the authority of Zirr, who said: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with him) said to me: "How many verses do you count in Surat al-Ahzab?" I said: "Seventy-three verses." He said: "By Him by whom Ubayy ibn Kaʿb swears, it was once equal to Surat al-Baqara or longer."

And we used to recite from it the verse of stoning: ﴿The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾. [Related by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh, all through this line of transmission.] Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) meant that this was among what was abrogated from the Qur'an. As for what is related, that this addition was in a sheet in the house of ʿAA'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), and a domestic animal ate it, it is among the fabrications of the heretics (al-malahida) and the Rafidites. [Note: Rather, its narrator is trustworthy and not accused. Ibrahim al-Harbi said in al-Gharib: Harun ibn ʿAbd Allah told us that the stoning verse was revealed in Surat al-Ahzab, written on a palm-leaf in the house of ʿA'isha, and her goat ate it. Abu Yaʿla, al-Daraqutni, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Maʿrifa all related it, all through the route of Muhammad ibn Ishaq from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr from ʿA'isha, and from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim from his father from ʿA'isha. End of quotation.] It seems the author understood that the establishment of this addition would imply what the Rafidites claim: that parts of the Qur'an were lost. This is not necessary; rather, this is among what had its recitation abrogated while its ruling remained. The eating of it by domestic animals occurred after the abrogation.

He made his address to him with the Prophet and the Messenger, in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ and ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid﴾, and ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you﴾, and He left addressing him by his name, as He said: ﴿O Adam﴾, ﴿O Musa﴾, ﴿O Isa﴾, ﴿O Dawud﴾, as an honour for him and a dignification, and an exalting of his station and a proclaiming of his merit. If you say: if He did not place his name in the address, He did place it in the report in His saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ and ﴿Muhammad is only a Messenger﴾. I say: that is to teach people that he is the Messenger of Allah, and to instruct them to name him thus and call him by it, so there is no difference between address and report. Do you not see how the reports not intended for teaching and instruction mention him in a manner similar to the address: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾, and ﴿The Messenger said: "My Lord, my people have certainly taken this Qur'an as abandoned"﴾, ﴿Certainly in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾, ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾, ﴿Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾, and ﴿Even if they were believers in Allah and the Prophet﴾.

"Fear Allah": persist in what you are upon of piety, remain steadfast in it, and increase in it, because piety is a door whose end is never reached. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾: do not support them in anything, do not accept from them an opinion or counsel, keep away from them and be on guard against them, for they are enemies of Allah and enemies of the believers, wanting nothing but harm and opposition.

It is related that when the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina, and he loved the conversion of the Jews of Qurayza, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa', and some of them had pledged allegiance to him in hypocrisy, he would lower his side to them, honour their young and old, and overlook any ugly conduct from them, and he would listen to them [I have not found it]. Then this was revealed.

It is related that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, ʿIkrima ibn Abi Jahl, and Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came to him under the truce that existed between him and them, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn Qays stood with them, and they said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Abandon mention of our gods, and say that they intercede and benefit, and we will leave you and your Lord." This was grievous to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to the believers, and they resolved to kill them [this is how al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned it, without a chain]. Then this was revealed: that is, fear Allah regarding breaking the covenant and abandoning the truce, and do not obey the disbelievers from the people of Mecca and the hypocrites from the people of Medina in what they request of you.

It is related that the people of Mecca invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to return from his religion, and they would give him half their wealth, and that he marry Shayba ibn Rabiʿa to his daughter; and the hypocrites of Medina frightened him that they would kill him if he did not return. Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of what is right from what is wrong, and of what is beneficial from what is corrupt, ﴿Wise﴾, who does nothing and commands nothing except by the motive of wisdom. ﴿And follow what is revealed to you﴾ in abandoning obedience to the disbelievers and hypocrites and other matters. ﴿Indeed Allah, who reveals to you, is Acquainted with what you do﴾, so He reveals to you what will set right your deeds, so you have no need to listen to the disbelievers. It was also read as "ya'malun" (with the letter ya'), meaning: by what the hypocrites do of their plotting against you and their scheming against you. ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾: entrust your affair to Him and commit yourself to His management, ﴿and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾: a guardian to whom every matter is entrusted.

God has not placed two hearts within a man's body, nor has He combined the status of wife and mother in one woman, nor the status of a true son and an adopted son (da'wah) in one man.

The meaning is this: just as God, glorified is He, in His wisdom did not see fit to give a human being two hearts—because it is not free of one of two possibilities: either the one does with each of them the same acts of the heart as the other does, so one of them is a superfluity not needed, or it does with one of them something other than what it does with the other, and that would lead to the whole being described as simultaneously willing and unwilling, knowing and conjecturing, certain and doubtful, in a single state—He likewise did not see fit that one woman should be both a mother to a man and his wife, because the mother is one served, to whom one lowers the wing of humility, while the wife is one employed, at whose disposal is the man's use of her for intercourse and other things, like a slave-woman; these are two mutually contradictory states. Nor should one man be both an adopted son (da'iy) of another man and his son, because true lineage (nubuwwah) is original in descent and rooted in it, whereas adoption (da'wah) is the attaching of an accidental designation to a name. [[Mahmud said: The finest of the interpretations mentioned here is that they used to say that Ibn Khatal had two hearts, so God denied the validity of that and coupled it with the contradictory sayings they used to utter, such as making adopted sons into sons and wives into mothers. He said: These three matters are mutually contradictory. As for the first, because the joining of two hearts entails that one of two opposing meanings subsists in one of them and its opposite in the other, as with knowledge and ignorance, security and fear, and so on. As for the second, because the wife is in a station of humiliation while the mother is in a place of honour, so it is contrary for the wife to be a mother. As for the third, because true lineage is original and rooted, whereas adoption is adhering and accidental, so the two are contradictory. He mentioned "the chest" (jawf) to depict the image of two hearts being joined within it, so that the hearer hastens to deny it.]] There is nothing else; and it is not possible for one thing to be both original and not original. This is an example God struck regarding Zayd ibn Harithah, who was a man from the tribe of Kalb, taken captive as a child. The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time used to raid and plunder one another. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his aunt Khadijah; when she married the Messenger of God (ﷺ), she gifted him to him. His father and uncle sought him, and he was given the choice, but he chose the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he freed him. They used to say: "Zayd ibn Muhammad." [[Thus Ibn Ishaq mentioned it, and Ibn Abi Khaythamah from his route. He added at its end: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was ten years older than him, so he adopted him." And on the authority of Salim, from his father, who said: "We did not call him anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad until God revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾." End of quotation. This addition is in the two Sahihs, from Salim ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, from his father: "We did not call Zayd ibn Harithah, the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ – the verse."]] Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse, and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you﴾. It was said: Abu Ma'mar was a man among the most retentive and narrating of the Arabs, so he was called "the man of two hearts." It was also said: he was Jamil ibn Asad al-Fihri, who used to say: "I have two hearts, with one of which I understand more than Muhammad does." It is narrated that he fled on the day of Badr, and passed by Abu Sufyan, who had one of his sandals hanging in his hand and the other on his foot. He said to him: "What has become of the people?" He replied: "They are between slain and fleeing." He said: "What is the matter with one of your sandals being on your foot and the other in your hand?" He replied: "I did not think except that they were both on my feet." So God refuted his statement and theirs, and struck it as an example regarding the zihar and adoption. On the authority of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: the hypocrites used to say: "Muhammad has two hearts," so God refuted them. It was said: he forgot in his prayer, so the Jews said: "He has two hearts: a heart with his companions, and a heart with you." On the authority of al-Hasan: it was revealed concerning the one who says: "A soul commands me and a soul forbids me."

The indefinite form in "rajul" (man), and the insertion of min (in the sense of comprehensiveness) before "qalbayn" (two hearts), are two emphases for the intended meaning, as if he had said: God has not made for the human race, nor for any one of them, two hearts at all within his body.

If you ask: what is the benefit of mentioning "the chest"? I say: its benefit is like the benefit in His saying: ﴿the hearts which are in the breasts﴾, namely the increase in the hearer's conception of the indicated meaning, for when he hears it he forms in himself an image of a chest containing two hearts, and so he is quicker to deny it.

It is read: al-lā'ī, with a yā' and a hamzah both kasra'd. [[His saying "it is read al-lā'ī with a yā' and hamzah both kasra'd" perhaps means two readings: one with a kasra'd yā' and the other with a kasra'd hamzah; but the yā' is not a pure yā', rather it is a softened hamzah pronounced between the hamzah and the yā'. The sum is: it is read al-lā'ī with a yā' sakin after the hamzah. And it is read al-lā' with a kasra'd hamzah without a yā'. And it is read al-lāy with a yā' resembling a kasra'd yā', which is the hamzah pronounced between bayn bayn. And it is read al-lāy with a sakin yā' after the alif without hamz. These are four readings for the word al-lā'ī wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, as in the commentary on al-Shatibiyyah. (ʿ)]] "Al-lā'ī" with a yā' sākinah after the hamzah. "Tuzāhirūn": from "zāhara"; "tazāharūn" (from tazāhara), meaning the same; "tuzhirūn" from "azhara", meaning "tazhir"; "tazharūn" from "zahara", meaning "zāhara," like 'aqd meaning 'aqid; "tazharūn" from "zahara" in the verbal form of "zuhūr" (appearance). The meaning of "zāhara min imra'atihi" is: he said to her: "You are upon me like the back of my mother." Similarly in expression of the utterance: "labbā al-muhrim" when he says "labbayk," and "uffa al-rajul" when he says "uff," and its sisters. If you ask: what is the reason for its transitive form with min and its sisters? I say: zihār was divorce in the view of the people of the Jahiliyyah, so they would avoid the woman zihar-ed as they avoid a divorced woman. So their saying "tazāhara minhā" means he distanced himself from her by way of zihār; "tazhara minhā" means he guarded himself from her; "zāhara minhā" means he was wary of her; "zahara minhā" means he shrank from her; and "zahara minhā" means he freed himself from her. Its parallel is "ā'la min imra'atihi": since it implies the sense of distancing from her, it takes min; otherwise "ā'la," in its original meaning of swearing an oath, does not carry this ruling.

If you ask: what is the meaning of their saying: "You are upon me like the back of my mother"? I say: they wanted to say: "You are unlawful to me like the belly of my mother," but they used the back as a metaphor for the belly, so as not to mention the belly, because mentioning the belly comes close to mentioning the private part. They used the back as a metaphor for the belly only because it is the spine of the belly. From it is the hadith of Umar, may God be pleased with him: "One of them comes with it upon the spine of his belly," meaning upon his back. Another explanation: coming to a woman with her back towards the sky was forbidden and prohibited among them, and the people of Medina used to say: "If you come to a woman with her face to the ground, the child will be cross-eyed." So, to emphasise the severity of his prohibition of his wife to himself, the one who made zihār likened her to the back, then was not content with that, until he made her the back of his mother, leaving nothing further.

If you ask: "al-da'iy" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning one who is claimed as a son; why is its plural on the pattern af'ila'? The pattern of this type, when it means fa'il, as in taqi/atqiya' and shaqi/ashqiya', is correct, but this does not occur in forms such as ramā and sammā. I say: its deviation from analogy is like the deviation of qatlā' and asrā'; the way to deal with such cases is lexical resemblance. ﴿That is your saying by your mouths﴾: "This is my son," without any belief in its validity or its being true. God, mighty and majestic, does not say except what is true outwardly and inwardly, and He guides only to the path of truth. Then He said what is true and guided to what is the path of truth, which is His saying: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾, and He made clear that calling them by their fathers is the more equitable and just of the two matters. In the separation and connection of these sentences there is eloquence and excellence that is not hidden from a scholar of the ways of composition. Qatadah recited: ﴿And He it is who guides to the way﴾. It was said: a man in the Jahiliyyah, if he liked a man's sturdiness and grace, would take him to himself and give him a share like a male child's portion of his inheritance, and he would be attributed to him, so it would be said: "So-and-so son of so-and-so." ﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients﴾; so say: "This is my brother, and this is my client," and "O my brother," and "O my client," meaning brotherhood in religion and clientship in it. ﴿What your hearts have intended﴾ is in the genitive place, conjoined to ﴿what you have erred in﴾. It may also be in the nominative, as a beginning, with the predicate omitted, its estimated sense being: "But what your hearts have intended is the sin." The meaning: there is no sin upon you for what you did of that in error and ignorance before the prohibition arrived, but the sin is in what you intended after the prohibition.

Or: there is no sin upon you if you say to another's child "O my son" by way of error and slip of the tongue, but if you say it deliberately. It may also be meant that pardon applies to error and not to intention, in a general way, like his peace and blessings be upon him saying: "I do not fear for you error, but I fear for you intention." [[Reported by Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, from the route of Ja'far ibn Burqan, from Yazid ibn al-Asamm, from Abu Hurayrah, raised, more complete than it. Al-Tabarani reported it in al-Awsat and in Musnad al-Shamiyyin, from the narration of Thabit ibn Ajlan: "Ata' related to me from A'ishah, may God be pleased with her."]] And his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "God has removed from my community error, forgetfulness, and what they were compelled to." [[Reported by Ibn Adi from the narration of Hasan ibn Barqah, from his father, from al-Hasan, from Abu Bakrah, raised: "God has lifted from this community three things: error, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do." These are among the odd reports of Ja'far. Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban reported it from a hadith of Ibn Abbas. As for Ibn Hibban, he said: from Ata' from Ubayd ibn Umayr from him, with the wording "Indeed God has overlooked"; as for Ibn Majah, he said from al-Awza'i "Indeed God has removed".]] Then, by its generality, he included the error of adoption and its intention.

If you ask: when adoption occurs, what is its ruling? I say: if the adopted one is of unknown lineage and younger in age than the adopter, his lineage is established from him; and if he was a slave of his, he is freed along with the establishment of lineage. If one of his like cannot be born to one like him, the lineage is not established, but he is freed according to Abu Hanifah, may God the Exalted have mercy on him; according to his two companions, he is not freed. As for one of known lineage, his lineage is not established by adoption, even if he was a slave, he is freed. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾: for His pardon of error and of intention when the one who intends repents. [[His saying "and of intention when the one who intends repents" is the view of the Mu'tazilah; the Sunnis hold that He may forgive by bare grace.]]

God has not placed two hearts within a man's body, nor has He combined the status of wife and mother in one woman, nor the status of a true son and an adopted son (da'wah) in one man.

The meaning is this: just as God, glorified is He, in His wisdom did not see fit to give a human being two hearts—because it is not free of one of two possibilities: either the one does with each of them the same acts of the heart as the other does, so one of them is a superfluity not needed, or it does with one of them something other than what it does with the other, and that would lead to the whole being described as simultaneously willing and unwilling, knowing and conjecturing, certain and doubtful, in a single state—He likewise did not see fit that one woman should be both a mother to a man and his wife, because the mother is one served, to whom one lowers the wing of humility, while the wife is one employed, at whose disposal is the man's use of her for intercourse and other things, like a slave-woman; these are two mutually contradictory states. Nor should one man be both an adopted son (da'iy) of another man and his son, because true lineage (nubuwwah) is original in descent and rooted in it, whereas adoption (da'wah) is the attaching of an accidental designation to a name. [[Mahmud said: The finest of the interpretations mentioned here is that they used to say that Ibn Khatal had two hearts, so God denied the validity of that and coupled it with the contradictory sayings they used to utter, such as making adopted sons into sons and wives into mothers. He said: These three matters are mutually contradictory. As for the first, because the joining of two hearts entails that one of two opposing meanings subsists in one of them and its opposite in the other, as with knowledge and ignorance, security and fear, and so on. As for the second, because the wife is in a station of humiliation while the mother is in a place of honour, so it is contrary for the wife to be a mother. As for the third, because true lineage is original and rooted, whereas adoption is adhering and accidental, so the two are contradictory. He mentioned "the chest" (jawf) to depict the image of two hearts being joined within it, so that the hearer hastens to deny it.]] There is nothing else; and it is not possible for one thing to be both original and not original. This is an example God struck regarding Zayd ibn Harithah, who was a man from the tribe of Kalb, taken captive as a child. The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time used to raid and plunder one another. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his aunt Khadijah; when she married the Messenger of God (ﷺ), she gifted him to him. His father and uncle sought him, and he was given the choice, but he chose the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he freed him. They used to say: "Zayd ibn Muhammad." [[Thus Ibn Ishaq mentioned it, and Ibn Abi Khaythamah from his route. He added at its end: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was ten years older than him, so he adopted him." And on the authority of Salim, from his father, who said: "We did not call him anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad until God revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾." End of quotation. This addition is in the two Sahihs, from Salim ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, from his father: "We did not call Zayd ibn Harithah, the freedman of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ – the verse."]] Then God, mighty and majestic, revealed this verse, and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you﴾. It was said: Abu Ma'mar was a man among the most retentive and narrating of the Arabs, so he was called "the man of two hearts." It was also said: he was Jamil ibn Asad al-Fihri, who used to say: "I have two hearts, with one of which I understand more than Muhammad does." It is narrated that he fled on the day of Badr, and passed by Abu Sufyan, who had one of his sandals hanging in his hand and the other on his foot. He said to him: "What has become of the people?" He replied: "They are between slain and fleeing." He said: "What is the matter with one of your sandals being on your foot and the other in your hand?" He replied: "I did not think except that they were both on my feet." So God refuted his statement and theirs, and struck it as an example regarding the zihar and adoption. On the authority of Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: the hypocrites used to say: "Muhammad has two hearts," so God refuted them. It was said: he forgot in his prayer, so the Jews said: "He has two hearts: a heart with his companions, and a heart with you." On the authority of al-Hasan: it was revealed concerning the one who says: "A soul commands me and a soul forbids me."

The indefinite form in "rajul" (man), and the insertion of min (in the sense of comprehensiveness) before "qalbayn" (two hearts), are two emphases for the intended meaning, as if he had said: God has not made for the human race, nor for any one of them, two hearts at all within his body.

If you ask: what is the benefit of mentioning "the chest"? I say: its benefit is like the benefit in His saying: ﴿the hearts which are in the breasts﴾, namely the increase in the hearer's conception of the indicated meaning, for when he hears it he forms in himself an image of a chest containing two hearts, and so he is quicker to deny it.

It is read: al-lā'ī, with a yā' and a hamzah both kasra'd. [[His saying "it is read al-lā'ī with a yā' and hamzah both kasra'd" perhaps means two readings: one with a kasra'd yā' and the other with a kasra'd hamzah; but the yā' is not a pure yā', rather it is a softened hamzah pronounced between the hamzah and the yā'. The sum is: it is read al-lā'ī with a yā' sakin after the hamzah. And it is read al-lā' with a kasra'd hamzah without a yā'. And it is read al-lāy with a yā' resembling a kasra'd yā', which is the hamzah pronounced between bayn bayn. And it is read al-lāy with a sakin yā' after the alif without hamz. These are four readings for the word al-lā'ī wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, as in the commentary on al-Shatibiyyah. (ʿ)]] "Al-lā'ī" with a yā' sākinah after the hamzah. "Tuzāhirūn": from "zāhara"; "tazāharūn" (from tazāhara), meaning the same; "tuzhirūn" from "azhara", meaning "tazhir"; "tazharūn" from "zahara", meaning "zāhara," like 'aqd meaning 'aqid; "tazharūn" from "zahara" in the verbal form of "zuhūr" (appearance). The meaning of "zāhara min imra'atihi" is: he said to her: "You are upon me like the back of my mother." Similarly in expression of the utterance: "labbā al-muhrim" when he says "labbayk," and "uffa al-rajul" when he says "uff," and its sisters. If you ask: what is the reason for its transitive form with min and its sisters? I say: zihār was divorce in the view of the people of the Jahiliyyah, so they would avoid the woman zihar-ed as they avoid a divorced woman. So their saying "tazāhara minhā" means he distanced himself from her by way of zihār; "tazhara minhā" means he guarded himself from her; "zāhara minhā" means he was wary of her; "zahara minhā" means he shrank from her; and "zahara minhā" means he freed himself from her. Its parallel is "ā'la min imra'atihi": since it implies the sense of distancing from her, it takes min; otherwise "ā'la," in its original meaning of swearing an oath, does not carry this ruling.

If you ask: what is the meaning of their saying: "You are upon me like the back of my mother"? I say: they wanted to say: "You are unlawful to me like the belly of my mother," but they used the back as a metaphor for the belly, so as not to mention the belly, because mentioning the belly comes close to mentioning the private part. They used the back as a metaphor for the belly only because it is the spine of the belly. From it is the hadith of Umar, may God be pleased with him: "One of them comes with it upon the spine of his belly," meaning upon his back. Another explanation: coming to a woman with her back towards the sky was forbidden and prohibited among them, and the people of Medina used to say: "If you come to a woman with her face to the ground, the child will be cross-eyed." So, to emphasise the severity of his prohibition of his wife to himself, the one who made zihār likened her to the back, then was not content with that, until he made her the back of his mother, leaving nothing further.

If you ask: "al-da'iy" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning one who is claimed as a son; why is its plural on the pattern af'ila'? The pattern of this type, when it means fa'il, as in taqi/atqiya' and shaqi/ashqiya', is correct, but this does not occur in forms such as ramā and sammā. I say: its deviation from analogy is like the deviation of qatlā' and asrā'; the way to deal with such cases is lexical resemblance. ﴿That is your saying by your mouths﴾: "This is my son," without any belief in its validity or its being true. God, mighty and majestic, does not say except what is true outwardly and inwardly, and He guides only to the path of truth. Then He said what is true and guided to what is the path of truth, which is His saying: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾, and He made clear that calling them by their fathers is the more equitable and just of the two matters. The Prophet is closer to the believers than they are to themselves in every matter of religion and worldly affairs, and for this reason it was stated without restriction. Therefore it is obligatory upon them that he be more beloved to them than their own selves, and his judgment more binding upon them than their own judgment, and his right more preferred to them than their own rights, and their compassion for him more prior than their compassion for themselves; and that they should sacrifice themselves instead of him and make themselves a ransom for him when a matter becomes grave, and a shield for him when war rages; and that they should not follow what their souls call them to, nor what turns them away from him, but follow everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) calls them to and everything that turns them away from it. For everything he calls them to is guidance for them toward attaining salvation and victory with the happiness of both abodes, and everything that turns them away from it, he takes hold of them by their waistbands [[His words "fa-akhadha yahjizuhum" — in al-Sihah: "hujzat al-izar" is its knot, and "hujzat al-sarawil" is the place where the drawstring is. (Ea.)]] lest they fall headlong into what leads them to wretchedness and the punishment of the Fire. Or it means that he is more fitting for them, in the sense that he is more compassionate toward them, more tender to them, and more beneficial for them, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: "Toward the believers he is kind and merciful." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no believer except that I am closer to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves.' So whichever believer dies and leaves wealth, his heirs, whoever they may be, shall inherit it; and if he leaves debt or dependents, then they come to me." [[Related by al-Bukhari through the chain of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi ʿAmra from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, with similar meaning.]] In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them." Mujahid said: every prophet is the father of his community. That is why the believers became brothers, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is their father in religion. "And his wives are their mothers" is a comparison of them to mothers in some rulings, namely the obligation to honor and respect them and the prohibition of marrying them. Allah, the Exalted, said: "Nor is it for you to marry his wives after him, ever." Beyond that, they are in the position of non-related women. For this reason ʿA’isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "We are not the mothers of women." [[Related by al-Daraqutni from the narration of Mudarr al-A'tiq, who said: "Harfa' told me: I said to ʿA’isha, 'O mother—' and she said, 'I am not the mother of women; I am only the mother of men.'" In al-Tabaqat, through Masruq, who said: "A woman said to ʿA’isha, 'O mother—' and ʿA’isha said, 'I am not your mother; I am only the mother of men.'"]] She means that they were only mothers of men, because they are forbidden to them just as their mothers are forbidden. The evidence for this is that this prohibition did not extend to their daughters, and likewise the full rulings of mothers did not apply to them. In the early days of Islam, Muslims inherited from one another through the bond of allegiance in religion and through emigration, not through kinship, just as the hearts of some people were won over by giving them shares in the alms; then this was abrogated when Islam had become strong [[His words "lamma dajā al-Islām" — in al-Sihah: "dajā al-Islām" means it grew strong and covered everything. (Ea.)]] and its people were honored, and inheritance was made by the right of kinship. "In the Book of Allah" refers to the Preserved Tablet, or to what Allah revealed to His Prophet, which is this verse, or to the verse of inheritance, or to what Allah has prescribed, as in His words: "The Book of Allah is prescribed for you."

"From the believers and the emigrants" may be an explanation of "those of kinship," meaning: the relatives among these are more entitled than the strangers. It may also be for the beginning of the end, meaning: those of kinship, by the right of blood, are more entitled to inheritance than the believers by the right of allegiance in religion, and than the emigrants by the right of emigration.

If you ask: what is the exception in "unless you do" (illā an tafʿalū) excepting? I say: it is an exception from the general sense of benefit and kindness, as you would say: "The relative is more entitled than the stranger, except in the bequest." You mean that he has more right than him in every benefit, such as inheritance, gift, present, charity, and other things, except in the bequest. What is meant by "doing good" here is the bequest, since there is no bequest to an heir. The verb "tafʿalū" is construed with "ilā," because it carries the meaning of "tasdū" and "tazillū" [[His words "because it carries the meaning of tasdū and tazillū" — in al-Sihah: "azaltu ilayhi niʿmah" means I bestowed a favor upon him. And in the hadith: "Whoever has a favor bestowed upon him, let him thank it." (Ea.)]]. By "the allies" is meant the believers and the emigrants, by the bond of allegiance in religion. "That" refers to what has been mentioned in both verses together. The explanation of "the Book" is what passed just above, and the sentence is a fresh statement, serving as a conclusion to the rulings that have been mentioned.

﴿And remember when We took from the prophets their covenant, all of them, to convey the message and to call to the upright religion, and from you in particular, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus﴾. We did this so that Allah would question, on the Day of Resurrection, at the gathering of the witnesses, the believers who fulfilled their covenant and kept it. They were among those whom He made witness against themselves, saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes, we testify﴾. He would question them about the truthfulness of their covenant and their testimony, and the prophets would testify for them that they had been truthful in their covenant and testimony and that they were believers. Or, He would question those who confirmed the prophets about their confirmation, for whoever says to the truthful one, "You have spoken the truth," is himself truthful in his statement. Or, He would question the prophets about what their nations answered them. The interpretation of the questioning of the messengers is a rebuke of the disbelievers who opposed them, like His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾

If you say: Why did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) precede Noah and those after him?

[[Mahmud said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was placed before Noah because they mentioned a specification after a generalization, as a distinction for them, so he placed the most excellent of those specified." Ahmad said: "Precedence in mention does not necessarily imply this. Do you not see his saying:

Among them in Layl are Ja'far and the son of his mother,
'Ali, and among them Ahmad, the chosen one.

So the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) was delayed so that it would be concluded with it, as an honour to him. And if it is established that excellence is not necessarily implied by precedence, then the secret of placing him (ﷺ) before Noah and those after him in mention becomes apparent, and Allah knows best: he is the one addressed among them, and this recited Book was revealed to him, so his precedence was for this reason. Then, when he (ﷺ) was placed first in mention, the mention of the prophets, may Allah bless them, followed in the order of their times of existence, and Allah knows best."]]

I say: This conjunction is to show the excellence of the prophets, who are the most renowned of them and their descendants. [[His words "they are their famous ones and their descendants" are perhaps "their luminaries" with a dal, and the "darari" (luminaries) are the great stars, as the Sihah (a lexicon) states. (ʿAyn)]]. Since Muhammad (ﷺ) is the most excellent of these excellent ones, he was placed before them to show that he is the most excellent of them. Had it not been so, the one whose time was earlier would have been placed first.

If you say: Noah was placed before him in the verse that is the sister of this verse, namely His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We revealed to you﴾, and then (the others) were placed after him. I say: The manner in which this verse is presented differs from the manner of that one. Allah the Exalted only mentioned it to describe the religion of Islam as original and upright. It is as if He said: He has prescribed for you the original religion upon which Noah was sent in the ancient age, and upon which Muhammad, the seal of the prophets, was sent in the recent age, and upon which were sent those famous prophets who came between them.

If you say: What did He intend by the "firm covenant"? I say: He intended by it that same covenant. Its meaning: We took from them by that covenant a firm covenant. Firmness (ghilaz) is a metaphor drawn from the description of physical bodies, and what is meant is the greatness of the covenant and the nobility of its status in its domain. It has also been said that the "firm covenant" is the oath by Allah to fulfil what they were entrusted with.

If you say: To what is His saying ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers﴾ conjoined? I say: It is conjoined to "We took from the prophets," because the meaning is that Allah emphasized upon the prophets the call to His religion in order to reward the believers, and He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment. Or it is conjoined to what is indicated by ﴿that He may question the truthful﴾, as if He said: So He rewarded the believers and prepared for the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verses 9–11:

﴿Remember the favour of God upon you when armies came against you﴾: that is, the Day of the Confederates (Yawm al-Ahzab), which is the Day of the Trench (Yawm al-Khandaq), ﴿when armies came against you﴾, namely the Confederates (al-Ahzab). So God sent against them the east wind (rih al-saba).

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I was given victory by the east wind, and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind." [Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father.]

God sent upon them a cold wind on a wintry night, which ﴿fakhsaratahum﴾ [[The word "fakhsaratahum" in al-Sihah: "al-khasr" with a vowel on the kha' means cold. And "khasara al-rajul" means: when cold afflicted his extremities. So "fakhsaratahum" means: it put them into al-khasr, i.e. cold. (Gh.)]] — it struck them with cold and blew dust into their faces. The angels were commanded, and they uprooted the tent pegs, cut the tent ropes, extinguished the fires, overturned the cooking pots, the horses collided with one another, terror was cast into their hearts, and the angels shouted takbir (Allahu akbar) on the sides of their camp.

Then Talha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi said: "As for Muhammad, he has begun you with magic, so save yourselves, save yourselves!" And they fled without any fighting.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard of their advance, he dug the trench around Medina; Salman al-Farisi, may God be pleased with him, had advised him to do so. Then he went out with three thousand of the Muslims and pitched his camp, with the trench between him and the enemy. He commanded that the children and women be raised up into the fortresses (al-atam) [[The phrase "fa-rufi'u fi al-atam": "al-atam" means the fortresses, plural of "atam" on the pattern of "'unuq". The Quraysh had advanced with ten thousand men from the Ahabish, the Banu Kinanah and the people of Tihamah, and their commander was Abu Sufyan. Ghatafan went out with a thousand and those who followed them from the people of Najd, their commander being 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn, and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl among Hawazin. ﴿From above you﴾: from the upper part of the valley, from the direction of the east: the Banu Ghatafan. ﴿And from below you﴾: from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west: the Quraysh. They formed a confederacy and said: "We shall be one body until we uproot Muhammad."

﴿And when the eyes were dazzled (zaghati al-absar)﴾: they deviated from their customary course and the level of their gaze, through bewilderment and staring.

It was said: they turned away from everything and looked at nothing but their enemy, because of the intensity of terror. The hanjarah is the top of the adam's apple (al-ghalsamah), which is the end of the throat (al-halqum). The halqum is the passage of food and drink. They said: when the lungs swell from intense fear, anger or severe grief, they puff up, and the heart rises with their rising to the top of the throat; hence it is said of a coward: "his lungs have swollen." It is permissible that this is a metaphor for the agitation and pounding of hearts, even though they did not literally reach the throats.

﴿And you thought about God with thoughts﴾: this is addressed to those who believed. Among them were the steadfast in heart and foot, and the weak in heart, those who are on an edge, and the hypocrites, who had faith only with their tongues. The first group thought that God was testing and trying them, so they feared slipping and weakness of endurance; as for the others, they thought about God what is related of them. It is related from al-Hasan: they had various thoughts: the hypocrites thought the Muslims would be annihilated, and the believers thought they were being tested.

It is read "al-zunun" without an alif in pause and in continuation, which is the analogical reading, and with an added alif in pause, which they added for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah), as one who added it in the rhyme (qafiyah) said:

Al-Zamakhshari said: when the reciter continues and does not pause, and the apparent statement of the grammarians is that it occurs only in pause. He made the anger of Banu Tamim the anger of all people, because whoever is other than them follows them, or is as if non-existent.

It is also narrated: "idha ghadibat 'alayka" (when I am angry with you), and the address is to every listener.]]

And likewise ﴿the Messenger﴾ and ﴿the way﴾ (al-rasula wa al-sabila). It is also read with the addition of the alif in continuation too, treating it as if it were in pause. Abu 'Ubayd said: all of them in the Imam (the standard codex) have the alif. From Abu 'Amr: the ishmam of the zay in "zulzilu" (they were shaken). It is read "zilzalan" with a fatha. The meaning is that fear unsettled them with the most severe unsettling.

﴿Had it been entered upon them﴾ from ﴿its sides﴾, from all its surroundings. It is said: "I entered upon so-and-so's house," and the meaning is: even if these gathered armies, from which they flee in fear, had entered their city and their houses from all its sides.

﴿They would have been drawn to it﴾ (*wa-inthāla*, "and they were poured out") upon their families and children, plundering and taking captives. Then, at that moment of terror and trembling, they were asked for ﴿the strife﴾, that is, apostasy, returning to disbelief, and fighting the Muslims. ﴿They would have brought it﴾ means they would have come to it and done it.

It is also read as ﴿*la-ātawhā*﴾ (*ātawhā*, "they would have given it"), meaning they would have given it. ﴿And they would not have delayed in it﴾, that is, they would not have delayed in giving it, ﴿except briefly﴾, just as long as it takes for the question and answer to be exchanged without any hesitation. Or it means: and they would not have remained in Madinah after their apostasy except briefly, for Allah would destroy them.

The meaning is: they offer excuses about the weakness of their houses, and they contrive pretexts so that they may flee from supporting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and from confronting the confederates whose hearts were filled with terror and dread. These confederates, if they had raided their land and homes, and had the disbelief offered to them, and been told to side against the Muslims, would have hastened to it without making any excuse. That is nothing other than their hatred of Islam, their intense enmity toward its people, their love of disbelief, and their eagerness for the party that holds it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 15–16:

From Ibn ʿAbbas: they pledged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of ʿAqaba that they would protect him in the same way they protect themselves. It was also said: they were a people who were absent from Badr, and they said: "If Allah makes us witness fighting, we will surely fight." And from Muhammad ibn Ishaq: they pledged on the day of Uhud that they would not flee after what had come down concerning them, [the pledge being] a matter that will be called to account (masʾūlan), something demanded (maṭlūban), a binding obligation (muqtaḍan) until it is fulfilled. ﴿Flight will not benefit you, if you flee from death or slaughter, [since] it is something you must encounter when it comes upon you, whether by natural death or by being killed.﴾ And if flight were to benefit you for a while, and you were granted respite by delay, that enjoyment would only be for a short time. And from one of the Marwanids: that he passed by a leaning wall and hurried past it, so this verse was recited to him, and he said: "It is that little time that we seek."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 17:

If you ask: how did he make mercy the counterpart of harm in "protection," when protection is only from harm? I answer: the meaning is "or He afflicts you with harm if He intends mercy for you." The speech has been abbreviated and treated like the poet's line:

"And I saw your husband in the battle-din, / girding on a sword and a spear" [The poem: "ورأيت زوجك في الوغى ... متقلدا سيفا ورمحا"

al-Wughā (الوغى): war. Wa-rumḥan (ورمحا): an accusative governed by an implied verb that suits it, i.e., "girding on a sword and bearing a spear." It is also transmitted with the first hemistich replaced by: "Would that your husband had set out" (يا ليت زوجك قد غدا), i.e., he went to war in the morning, wearing his weapons.]

Or the second clause is made to follow the first, because "protection" carries the sense of prevention.

Those who discourage (al-Mu'awwiqin): the hypocrites who dissuaded people from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They would say to their brethren, the residents of Madinah among the Ansar of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Muhammad and his companions are nothing but a morsel for the head" [[His saying "Muhammad and his companions are nothing but a morsel for the head" means: they are few, such that one head would satisfy them; it is the plural of ākil (eater). Al-iltihām is swallowing, as in al-Sihah. (ʿIyad)]], "and if they were flesh, Abu Sufyan and his companions would devour them. So leave them, and come to us (halumma ilayna)," meaning: bring yourselves close to us. This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, who use it uniformly for the singular and the plural. As for Tamim, they say: halumma ya rajul (to a man), and halumma ya rijal (to men). It is a sound named as a transitive verb, like uhdur (come) and qarrib (bring near). "Say: Bring your witnesses" (Qur'an 6:150), "except a little": except coming a little. They go out with the believers, giving them the impression that they are with them, but we do not see them fighting or engaging in combat, except a little when compelled to, like His saying: "They did not fight except a little" (Qur'an 33:18 variant reading in this context). "Grudging toward you": in the time of war, stingy about you, flapping around you as a man does with one he protects, defending him against the one who attacks him in fear. "You see them looking at you" in that state like one who is faint from the throes of death, out of fear and cowardice. "But when fear departs and the spoils are collected and the division is made, they transfer that stinginess, that grudging and that flapping around you, to the good, which is wealth and booty, and forget that first state. They become bold against you and strike you with their tongues, saying: 'Give us our share, for we have witnessed you and fought with you, and by our presence you prevailed over your enemy and by us you were given victory over them.'" Grudgingly (ashihhatan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, or as a term of dispraise. It is also read ashihhatun in the nominative. Wa-salaqukum is read with the sad. If you ask: Can a hypocrite be credited with any deed so that nullification (ihbat) applies to him? I say: No. But this is a teaching for whoever might suppose that faith by the tongue is faith even if the heart does not settle in it, and that what the hypocrite does of deeds benefits him. So it makes clear that his faith is not faith, and that every deed proceeding from him is void. It also urges the responsible person to perfect the foundation of his affair, which is sound faith, and it alerts that many deeds without correct knowledge are like building without a foundation, and that they go away with God as scattered dust. If you ask: What is the meaning of His saying: "And that is with God easy" (33:30), when everything is easy for Him? I say: The meaning is that their deeds are truly deserving of nullification, which their motives call for, and nothing turns it aside. "They think the confederates have not withdrawn," though they had withdrawn and returned from the trench to Madinah because of the severe terror that befell them and the extreme cowardice that entered them. "And if the confederates come again" for a second time, they wish, out of their fear of what they were afflicted with, that they were out in the desert among the Bedouin, "asking about your news" of every arrival from the direction of Madinah about your reports and what befell you. "And if they were among you," not returning to Madinah, "they would fight only a little," merely a pretext ('illa ta'alla) for show and reputation. [[His saying "illa ta'alla": in al-Sihah, 'allalahu bi-shay'in means he diverted him with it, as a child is diverted with some food so that he forgets milk. One says: so-and-so occupies himself with a pretext. (ʿIyad)]] It is also read bidda, as fa'ul plural of bad, like ghaz and ghazzi. In the transmission of Sahib al-Iqlid it is bidday, on the pattern of 'adiyy. "Yas'alun" means "yatasa'alun" (ask one another), meaning: one says to another, "What did you hear? What reached you?" Or "yatasa'alun al-a'rab" (they ask the Bedouin), as you say: "I saw the crescent and we saw it together." It was incumbent upon you to console the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with your persons, support him, and stand firm with him, as he consoled you with his own person in patience in jihad and steadfastness in the place where the millstone of war turns, until his incisor was broken on the day of Uhud and his face was wounded. ["In the place where the millstone of war turns" means the place where its mill is run. (ʿIyad, from al-Sihah)]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 21:

If you ask: what is the real meaning of His words, ﴿Certainly you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent exemplar﴾, and it has been read as "uswah" with a damma (ḍamm)? [[His statement "and it has been read as uswah with a damma" indicates that the reading with a kasra is the well-known one. (ʿAynī)]] I answer: there are two aspects to it. The first is that it is itself an excellent exemplar, that is, a model (qudwah), and it is the one to be emulated (al-mūtasā), that is, the one who is followed, just as you say: "In the egg there are twenty mann of iron," meaning that it itself is this amount of iron. The second is that it contains a quality that is worthy of being emulated and followed, namely his consoling of himself (al-muwāsāh bi-nafsih). ﴿For those who hope for Allah﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿you﴾, like His words ﴿to those among them who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾, [who hope for Allah and the Last Day]: from your saying "I hoped for Zayd and his bounty," that is, the bounty of Zayd. Or it means "hoping for the days of Allah," especially the Last Day. Hope here means either expectation or fear, and ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾ joins hope with abundant acts of worship and devotion to righteous deeds. The one who emulates the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is one who is like this.

Almighty God had promised them that they would be shaken, so that they would cry out to Him for help and seek His victory, as in His words: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ [2:214]. So when the confederates (al-Ahzab) came and bore down upon them, and they were agitated and struck with intense terror, they said: ﴿This is what God and His Messenger promised us﴾ [33:22], and they became certain of Paradise and of victory.

It is related on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his Companions: "The confederates are marching toward you after nine or ten [days]," meaning: at the end of nine or ten nights. When they saw them approaching at the appointed time, they said that [[I have not found this]]. This is an indication of the calamity or trial, (accepted) with faith in God and in His promises, and with submission to His decrees and His predestination.

Some of the Companions vowed that if they encountered battle alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they would stand firm and fight until they were martyred. They were: ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah, and Saʿid ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl,

and Hamzah, Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. ﴿Among them are those who have fulfilled their vow﴾ — meaning Hamzah and Musʿab — ﴿and among them are those who await﴾ — meaning ʿUthman and Talhah. And in a hadith: "Whoever wishes to look at a martyr walking upon the face of the earth, let him look at Talhah." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim through the route of al-Salt ibn Dinar from Abu Nadrah from Jabir. Al-Salt is weak, and there is another route in al-Tabarani through the sons of Talhah from Talhah.]] If you ask: What is qada' al-nahb (fulfilling the vow)? I answer: It is an expression for death, because every living being must die. It is as if he had a binding vow upon his neck; when he dies, he has fulfilled his vow, i.e., his pledge. His words ﴿Among them are those who have fulfilled their vow﴾ may mean that he died as a martyr, and may mean that he fulfilled his vow of standing firm with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If you ask: What is the real meaning of His words ﴿They have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾?

I answer: It is said, "Your brother was truthful to me and lied to me," when he told you the truth or a lie. As for the proverb, "The age of his camel truly informed me" (ṣadaqanī sinn bakrih), its meaning is: it was truthful to me regarding the age of its young camel, with the preposition omitted and the verb made to reach its object. So either ﴿what they covenanted with Allah﴾ stands in the position of "sinn" with the preposition dropped, or the thing covenanted upon is made the thing "truly" affirmed, figuratively, as if they said to the covenanted matter: "We will fulfill you," and they were fulfilling it; so they have been true to it. Had they been breakers of covenant, they would have been lying to it, and it would have been a lie. ﴿And they have not altered the covenant at all﴾ — neither the one who was martyred nor the one who awaits martyrdom. Talhah stood firm with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud until his hand was struck, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Talhah has made Paradise obligatory." [[Narrated by al-Tha laba bi from the narration of Harir ibn Hazim from ʿUrwah regarding His words "Among the believers are men who were true..." — the verse — "among them Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah," and so he mentioned it. It has been transmitted separately through other routes. Its implication is that his hand was struck. Al-Bukhari narrated it from the narration of Qays ibn Abi Hazim: "I saw Talhah's hand withered, with which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) protected himself on the day of Uhud"; and al-Nasa'i through the route of ʿUmarah ibn Ghaziyyah from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir who said: "When it was the day of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in a corner with twelve men of the Ansar," and he mentioned the lengthy account. His words "Talhah has made it obligatory" were narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq, Abu Yaʿla and al-Bazzar through the route of Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr from his father with the same wording.]] In it is an allusion to those among the hypocrites who altered their covenant and had a sickness in their hearts: the hypocrites, by their alteration, seem to have intended and desired the evil end, just as the truthful intended the end of truthfulness by their fidelity, since both groups are driven toward their ends of reward and punishment; so it is as if the two were equal in their seeking and striving to attain them. ﴿And He punishes the hypocrites if He wills﴾ — if they do not repent — ﴿or turns to them in forgiveness﴾ — if they repent. ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved, [with] their rage, not having obtained any good﴾ — the factions — ﴿enraged﴾, like His words ﴿a tree growing with oil﴾. ﴿Not having obtained any good﴾, not victorious. The two are circumstantial clauses either by overlap or by succession. It is permissible that the second be an explanation of the first, or a new statement. ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ — by the wind and the angels. ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported the factions from their fortresses﴾ — from their strongholds. The ṣayṣiyah is that by which one fortifies oneself; it is said of the horn of a bull or a gazelle: ṣayṣiyah, and of the spur of a rooster, which is its claw on its leg, because it fortifies itself with it. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the morning of the night in which the factions were defeated and the Muslims returned to Madinah and laid down their weapons — on his horse, al-Haizum, with dust on the horse's face and on the saddle — and said: "What is this, O Jibril?" He said: "From pursuing Quraysh." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping the dust from the horse's face and from the saddle. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, the angels have not laid down their weapons. Allah commands you to march against Banu Qurayzah, and I am heading toward them; Allah will crush them as eggs are crushed upon the rock, and they will be a provision for you." So he proclaimed among the people that whoever was listening and obedient should not pray ʿAsr except in Banu Qurayzah. Many people did not pray ʿAsr until after ʿIshaʾ, owing to the Prophet's words. He besieged them for twenty-five nights until the siege exhausted them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Will you come down under my judgment?" They refused. He said: "Under the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh?" They agreed to it. Saʿd said: "I judge that their fighting men be killed, and their children and women be taken captive." The Prophet (ﷺ) exclaimed Allahu akbar and said: "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above seven heavens." [[His words "from above seven heavens" — in al-Sihah, "al-raqiʿ" is the lowest heaven, and likewise the rest of the heavens. In the hadith it is "from above seven raqiʿ," in the masculine form, as if he had in mind the ceiling. (ʿ)]] Then he made them come down, dug a trench in the market of Madinah, brought them forward and struck their necks; they numbered between eight hundred and nine hundred. It is said there were six hundred fighting men and seven hundred captives. [[This is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, in the account of the expedition of Banu Qurayzah, from Ibn Ishaq to the final figure; Ibn Ishaq traced it through ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar from ʿAbd al-Rahman, that ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, from ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas al-Laythi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said—and he mentioned it. and Hamzah, Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. ﴿Among them are those who have fulfilled their vow﴾ — meaning Hamzah and Musʿab — ﴿and among them are those who await﴾ — meaning ʿUthman and Talhah. And in a hadith: "Whoever wishes to look at a martyr walking upon the face of the earth, let him look at Talhah." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim through the route of al-Salt ibn Dinar from Abu Nadrah from Jabir. Al-Salt is weak, and there is another route in al-Tabarani through the sons of Talhah from Talhah.]] If you ask: What is qada' al-nahb (fulfilling the vow)? I answer: It is an expression for death, because every living being must die. It is as if he had a binding vow upon his neck; when he dies, he has fulfilled his vow, i.e., his pledge. His words ﴿Among them are those who have fulfilled their vow﴾ may mean that he died as a martyr, and may mean that he fulfilled his vow of standing firm with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If you ask: What is the real meaning of His words ﴿They have been true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾?

I answer: It is said, "Your brother was truthful to me and lied to me," when he told you the truth or a lie. As for the proverb, "The age of his camel truly informed me" (ṣadaqanī sinn bakrih), its meaning is: it was truthful to me regarding the age of its young camel, with the preposition omitted and the verb made to reach its object. So either ﴿what they covenanted with Allah﴾ stands in the position of "sinn" with the preposition dropped, or the thing covenanted upon is made the thing "truly" affirmed, figuratively, as if they said to the covenanted matter: "We will fulfill you," and they were fulfilling it; so they have been true to it. Had they been breakers of covenant, they would have been lying to it, and it would have been a lie. ﴿And they have not altered the covenant at all﴾ — neither the one who was martyred nor the one who awaits martyrdom. Talhah stood firm with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud until his hand was struck, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Talhah has made Paradise obligatory." [[Narrated by al-Tha laba bi from the narration of Harir ibn Hazim from ʿUrwah regarding His words "Among the believers are men who were true..." — the verse — "among them Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah," and so he mentioned it. It has been transmitted separately through other routes. Its implication is that his hand was struck. Al-Bukhari narrated it from the narration of Qays ibn Abi Hazim: "I saw Talhah's hand withered, with which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) protected himself on the day of Uhud"; and al-Nasa'i through the route of ʿUmarah ibn Ghaziyyah from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir who said: "When it was the day of Uhud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in a corner with twelve men of the Ansar," and he mentioned the lengthy account. His words "Talhah has made it obligatory" were narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq, Abu Yaʿla and al-Bazzar through the route of Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr from his father with the same wording.]] In it is an allusion to those among the hypocrites who altered their covenant and had a sickness in their hearts: the hypocrites, by their alteration, seem to have intended and desired the evil end, just as the truthful intended the end of truthfulness by their fidelity, since both groups are driven toward their ends of reward and punishment; so it is as if the two were equal in their seeking and striving to attain them. ﴿And He punishes the hypocrites if He wills﴾ — if they do not repent — ﴿or turns to them in forgiveness﴾ — if they repent. ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved, [with] their rage, not having obtained any good﴾ — the factions — ﴿enraged﴾, like His words ﴿a tree growing with oil﴾. ﴿Not having obtained any good﴾, not victorious. The two are circumstantial clauses either by overlap or by succession. It is permissible that the second be an explanation of the first, or a new statement. ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ — by the wind and the angels. ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Book who supported the factions from their fortresses﴾ — from their strongholds. The ṣayṣiyah is that by which one fortifies oneself; it is said of the horn of a bull or a gazelle: ṣayṣiyah, and of the spur of a rooster, which is its claw on its leg, because it fortifies itself with it. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the morning of the night in which the factions were defeated and the Muslims returned to Madinah and laid down their weapons — on his horse, al-Haizum, with dust on the horse's face and on the saddle — and said: "What is this, O Jibril?" He said: "From pursuing Quraysh." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping the dust from the horse's face and from the saddle. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, the angels have not laid down their weapons. Allah commands you to march against Banu Qurayzah, and I am heading toward them; Allah will crush them as eggs are crushed upon the rock, and they will be a provision for you." So he proclaimed among the people that whoever was listening and obedient should not pray ʿAsr except in Banu Qurayzah. Many people did not pray ʿAsr until after ʿIshaʾ, owing to the Prophet's words. He besieged them for twenty-five nights until the siege exhausted them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "Will you come down under my judgment?" They refused. He said: "Under the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh?" They agreed to it. Saʿd said: "I judge that their fighting men be killed, and their children and women be taken captive." The Prophet (ﷺ) exclaimed Allahu akbar and said: "You have judged by the judgment of Allah from above seven heavens." [[His words "from above seven heavens" — in al-Sihah, "al-raqiʿ" is the lowest heaven, and likewise the rest of the heavens. In the hadith it is "from above seven raqiʿ," in the masculine form, as if he had in mind the ceiling. (ʿ)]] Then he made them come down, dug a trench in the market of Madinah, brought them forward and struck their necks; they numbered between eight hundred and nine hundred. It is said there were six hundred fighting men and seven hundred captives. [[This is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, in the account of the expedition of Banu Qurayzah, from Ibn Ishaq to the final figure; Ibn Ishaq traced it through ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar from ʿAbd al-Rahman, that ʿUmar ibn Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, from ʿAlqamah ibn Waqqas al-Laythi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said—and he mentioned it. Abu Nuʿaym narrated in al-Dala'il through the route of Muʿadh ibn Rifaʿah from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged them, Jibril came to him while he was washing his head."]] It is read: al-raʿb, with the ʿayn sukun and with damma. And tasirun, with damma on the sin. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) made their properties belong to the Muhajirun to the exclusion of the Ansar; the Ansar spoke about that, and he said: "You have your dwellings." ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Will you not take a fifth as you took it on the day of Badr?" From Muqatil (may Allah be pleased with him): it is Khaybar. From ʿIkrimah: every land that will be conquered until the Day of Resurrection. And among the strange interpretations: that it means their women.

They desired some of the worldly life: clothing and extra provision, and they became jealous of one another. This grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then the verse was revealed. He began with ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who was the most beloved of them to him. He offered her the choice and recited the Qur'an to her, and she chose Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode. The joy was seen on the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then all of them chose as she had chosen, and Allah thanked them for that. So He revealed ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this, nor is it lawful to exchange them for other wives﴾ [33:52].

It is narrated that he said to ʿĀʾishah: "I am going to mention a matter to you, and there is no harm in your not hurrying over it until you consult your two parents." Then he recited the Qur'an to her. She said: "Is it about this that I should consult my parents? Indeed, I desire Allah, His Messenger, and the Last Abode." [Agreed upon, from the narration of al-Zuhri from Abu Salamah from ʿĀʾishah, with the addition: "Then the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) did as I did."]

It is also narrated that she said: "Do not inform your wives that I have chosen you." He said: "Allah sent me only as a conveyer of the message, not as one who makes things difficult." [Transmitted by Salim from the narration of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir concerning the story of the choice. At its end: "And I ask you to give choice to one of your wives, for no wife of yours asks me but that I inform her. Indeed, Allah did not send me as one who causes difficulty or seeks to make things difficult, but He sent me as a teacher who makes things easy." And in the two Sahihs, from the narration of Maʿmar from al-Zuhri from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah from Ibn ʿAbbas, the story is related at length. At its end in Muslim, Maʿmar said: "Ayyub informed us that ʿĀʾishah said to him: 'Do not inform your wives that I have chosen you.' He said: 'Indeed Allah sent me as a conveyer of the message, not as one who makes things difficult.'"]

If you ask: What is the ruling on choice (takhyīr) in divorce (ṭalāq)? I answer: If he says to her, "Choose," and she says, "I have chosen myself," or he says, "Choose yourself," and she says, "I have chosen," then it is necessary to mention the self in the words of the one who gives choice or the one who is given it. A single irrevocable divorce (bāʾin) takes effect according to Abu Hanifah and his companions. [Agreed upon, with both wordings.] And it is narrated: "Was it then a divorce?" It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: If she chooses her husband, it is one revocable divorce; and if she chooses herself, it is one irrevocable divorce. It is also narrated from him that if she chooses her husband, it is nothing.

The original sense of taʿālā is that one says it from a high place to someone in a lower place. Then its use spread until places became equal in its usage. The meaning of taʿālayna (ﷺ) is: come with your will and your choice to one of two matters. It does not mean that they should rise up toward him by themselves, as you say: "He came to argue with me," "He went to speak with me," "He stood to threaten me."

﴿I will provide for you and release you in a fair release﴾ [33:28]. I will give you the enjoyment of divorce (mutʿah). If you ask: Is the enjoyment (mutʿah) in divorce obligatory or not? I answer: For a divorced woman who has not been consummated with and for whom no dowry was fixed in the contract, her enjoyment is obligatory according to Abu Hanifah and his companions. As for the other divorced women, their enjoyment is recommended. It is narrated from al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with him, that there are two kinds of enjoyment: one is decreed by the ruler for one who divorces before fixing the dowry and before consummation; the second is a right upon the God-fearing (al-muttaqīn) for one who divorces after the dowry has been fixed and consummation has occurred. A woman brought a case to Shurayh concerning the enjoyment, and he said: "Provide for her, if you are one of the God-fearing," and he did not compel him. It is narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the enjoyment is a decreed right. It is narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: Every divorced woman has enjoyment except the one who redeems herself (mukhtalaʿah) and the one subjected to li'ān. The enjoyment consists of a shirt, a head-covering, and a wrapper, according to one's means and circumstances, except that if half her dowry is less than that, then the lesser of the two is due to her. It must not be less than five dirhams, because the minimum dowry is ten dirhams, so it must not fall below half of it.

Al-Fāḥisha (the flagrant indecency): the evil that is extremely ugly in its foulness, namely a major sin. Al-Mubayyina: that whose foulness is manifest. The intended meaning is every major sin they might commit. It has also been said that it is their disobedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their rebelliousness, and their asking of him for what would burden him or constrict his breast and grieve him on their account. It has also been said that it is fornication, but Allah protected His Messenger from that, as has passed in the hadith of the slander (ḥadīth al-ifk).

The reason their punishment was doubled is that what is ugly from the rest of women is less ugly than what is from them, and more ugly, because the increase in the ugliness of disobedience follows the increase in excellence, rank, and blessing upon the one who disobeys, from the one disobeyed. None of the women has the excellence of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and none of them has upon them a blessing like that which Allah has bestowed upon them. Recompense follows the act, and the recompense being a punishment follows the act being ugly; so whenever its ugliness increases, its punishment increases in severity. For this reason the condemnation by people of intellect of the knowing disobedient is more severe than of the ignorant disobedient, because disobedience from the knowing one is uglier. For this reason the punishment for free persons is greater than the punishment for slaves, to the extent that Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions do not hold that stoning applies to a disbeliever.

﴿And that was for Allah easy﴾ is an announcement that their being the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) does not avail them anything. How could it avail them when it is the cause of the doubling of the punishment? So it was a call to tightening the matter upon them, not a diversion from it.

Read: yaʾti (with tā' and yā'). Mubayyina: with fatḥa and kasra on the yā' (from bayyana in the sense of tabayyana). Yuḍāʿaf and yuḍʿaf: in the passive form. Yuḍāʿaf and nuḍʿaf: with yā' and nūn.

Also read: taqnut and taʿmal with tā' and yā'. Nu'tihā with yā' and nūn. Al-qunūt: obedience. Their reward was doubled because they sought the pleasure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through good character, good companionship, contentment, and their devotion to the worship of Allah and piety.
