Whoever makes "khalisah" a qualifier of the woman, then on his view: this woman is exclusively yours apart from them. "And God is Forgiving" to the one who falls into hardship if he repents, "Merciful" in extending ease to His servants.

It is narrated that when the Mothers of the Believers became jealous of one another, sought an increase in maintenance, and vexed the Messenger of God ﷺ, he abandoned them for a month, and the choice (al-takhyir) was revealed; they feared he would divorce them, so they said: "O Messenger of God, impose upon us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish." [This is a compilation of narrations. Its beginning, according to Muslim, through the route of Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "Abu Bakr entered upon the Prophet ﷺ while people were sitting at the door... the hadith," and in it the saying of Abu Bakr and Umar; he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ laughed and said: 'They are around me as you see, asking me for maintenance'—then he mentioned the hadith—and in it: 'So God revealed the verse of choice.'" And his saying, "he abandoned them for a month," is from the hadith of A'ishah in the two Sahihs. And his saying, "they feared he would divorce them—etc.," was narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah through the narration of Razin, that the Prophet ﷺ wished to part from his wives, and they said to him: "Apportion for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish, and leave us as we are." This is mursal. Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of Salim al-Aftas from Mujahid, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ had nine wives, and they feared that he would divorce them, so they said: 'O Messenger of God, apportion for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish, and do not divorce us.' Then the verse was revealed: 'You may defer whom you will of them...'"]

It is narrated that A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of God, I see your Lord hastening to fulfil your desire." [Agreed upon, from the hadith of Hisham from his father from A'ishah within a longer narration; al-Hakim erred and it was rectified by him.] "You may defer whom you will" — with hamz and without hamz — means: you may delay; "and take to yourself whom you will" means: you may join; that is: you may leave off lying with whom you will of them, and lie with whom you will. Or you may divorce whom you will and keep whom you will. Or you may not divorce, and you may apportion to whichever of them you will, and apportion to none; or you may leave off marrying whom you will of the women of your community, and marry whom you will. It is narrated from al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him: when the Prophet ﷺ proposed to a woman, no one was permitted to propose to her until he left her. This division is comprehensive of the purpose, for he either divorces or retains; if he retains, he lies with her or leaves her and apportions or does not apportion; and if he divorces and sets aside, then either he leaves the set-aside woman and does not seek her, or he seeks her. It is narrated that he deferred Sawdah, Juwayriyah, Safiyyah, Maymunah and Umm Habibah, and he apportioned to them whatever he willed, however he willed; and among those he took to himself were A'ishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab, may God be pleased with them; he deferred five and took four to himself. [Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah from Jarir, and by Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar, both from Mansur from Abu Razin; this is mursal.] It is narrated that he would equalise among those whom he was permitted to not apportion among, and offered the choice to, except Sawdah, for she gave up her night to A'ishah and said: "Do not divorce me until I am raised in the company of your wives." [As for his equalising, it is from A'ishah's hadith, "he apportioned and was just." As for the story of Sawdah, al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Abbas that "Sawdah feared the Messenger of God ﷺ would divorce her, so she said: 'O Messenger of God, do not divorce me; keep me, and give my day to A'ishah,' and he did so." In al-Tabarani, through the narration of Ibn Abi al-Zinad from Hisham from his father from A'ishah, she said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ did not prefer any of us over another in apportionment. Hardly a day passed without his circling us and approaching each of us without touching, until he reached the one whose day it was, and he would spend the night with her. Sawdah bint Zam'ah said to him, when he wished to part from her: 'My day is yours, and let me have A'ishah's.' He accepted this from her, and concerning her was revealed: 'And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion...'"]

"That delegation to your will is closer to comforting their eyes, to lessening their grief, and to all of them being content, because when he equalises among them in sheltering, deferring, setting aside and seeking, then distinction is removed, and none of them has in what she wants and what she does not want except the like of what the other has. When they know that this delegation is from God by His revelation, their souls are at rest, rivalry and jealousy depart, contentment is attained, eyes are comforted, and hearts are soothed." "And God knows what is in your hearts" — here is a warning to whoever among them is not content with what God has ordained and delegated to the will of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and an incitement to the harmony of their hearts, the purity of their relations with one another, and their agreement in seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of God ﷺ and that which brings contentment to his soul. It is read "tuqarra a'yunuhunna" with the tā' vowelled and the eyes in the accusative, and "taqarra a'yunuhunna" in the passive. "And God is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts, Forbearing" — who does not hasten punishment; so He is worthy to be feared and guarded against. "Kulluhunna" is an emphasis for the nūn of "yarḍayna" (they are content). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-yarḍayna kulluhunna bi-mā ātaytahunna" with the object fronted. And [another] read "kulluhunna" as an emphasis for "hunna" in "ātaytahunna."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 52:

﴿لَا يَحِلُّ﴾ It is also read in the masculine form (lā yaḥillu), because the feminine plural (of the noun) is not real (ḥaqīqī). If it is permissible without a separator, as in His words ﴿وَقَالَ نِسْوَةٌ﴾ ("And women said," 12:30), then with a separator it is more permissible. ﴿مِنْ بَعْدُ﴾ (after this): after the nine, because nine is the limit (niṣāb) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in wives, just as four is the limit of his community (ummah) in them. So it is not permissible for him to exceed the limit. ﴿وَلَا أَنْ تَبَدَّلَ بِهِنَّ﴾ nor to exchange them, that is, nor to substitute for these nine other wives, all of them or some of them. Allah willed for them honour and a reward for what they chose and were content with. So the Prophet ﷺ was restricted to them, and they are the nine whom he left behind at his death:

Ā'ishah bint Abī Bakr; Ḥafṣah bint 'Umar; Umm Ḥabībah bint Abī Sufyān; Sawdah bint Zam'ah; Umm Salamah bint Abī Umayyah; Ṣafiyyah bint Ḥuyayy al-Khaybariyyah; Maymūnah bint al-Ḥārith al-Hilāliyyah; Zaynab bint Jaḥsh al-Asadiyyah; Juwayriyyah bint al-Ḥārith al-Muṣṭaliqiyyah, may Allah be pleased with them.

[[The words "and they are the nine" are perhaps originally "and they are" (wa-hunna). (ʿ)]]

[[This is agreed upon, as al-Wāqidī and others said, but there is disagreement about Rayḥānah. Ibn Abī Khaythamah narrated from al-Zuhrī and from Qatādah, and Abū ʿUbayd said: "It is established with us and confirmed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Khadījah and did not marry another over her until she died. Then he married Sawdah, then ʿĀ'ishah, then Umm Salamah, then Ḥafṣah, then Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, then Juwayriyyah, then Umm Ḥabībah, then Ṣafiyyah, then Maymūnah, then Fāṭimah bint Surayj, then Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, then Hind bint Yazīd, then Asmāʾ bint al-Nuʿmān, then Hayla bint Qays, sister of al-Ashʿath, then Asmāʾ bint Sabaʾ." Al-Wāḥidī said: "The agreed view is that he married fourteen: the nine whom he left behind, and he also married Khadījah, Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, and Rayḥānah, and they died in his presence. He also married Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥaḥḥāk and Asmāʾ bint al-Nuʿmān, but he did not consummate the marriage with them."]]

﴿مِنْ أَزْوَاجٍ﴾ The min here is for emphasising the negation, and its benefit is that it encompasses the whole category of wives in the prohibition. It is also said that the meaning is: "Women are not lawful to you after the women whose lawfulness for you has been explicitly stated, from the four categories: the Bedouin women and the strangers, or the People of the Book, or the female slaves through marriage."

It is also said concerning the prohibition of exchange: it is from the exchange (badl) that was practised in the Jāhiliyyah, where a man would say to another, "Exchange your wife for mine, and I will exchange mine for yours," so each of them would step down from his wife for the other.

It is related that ʿUyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn entered upon the Prophet ﷺ while ʿĀ'ishah was with him, without asking permission. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O ʿUyaynah, where is the seeking of permission?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have not sought permission from any man of those who have passed since I came of age." Then he said: "Who is this beautiful one beside you?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "This is ʿĀ'ishah, the Mother of the Believers." ʿUyaynah said: "Shall I not step down for you from the best of creation?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, Allah has forbidden that." When he left, ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Who is this, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "A foolish man who is obeyed, and he, as you see, is the chief of his people."

[[Al-Bazzār narrated it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah with this wording and more complete, and in its chain is Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qarawī, who is abandoned (matrūk). It has a witness from the hadith of Jarīr narrated by al-Ṭabarānī, and another from ʿĀ'ishah narrated by Ibn Saʿd.]]

And from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her:

"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not die until women were made lawful to him." That is, the verse has been abrogated (nusikha).

[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, al-Nasāʾī, Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭabarī, al-Bazzār, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim from the hadith of ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, the hadith without the explanation. Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Saʿd narrated it from the hadith of Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her.]]

Its abrogation is either by the Sunnah, or by His words ﴿إِنَّا أَحْلَلْنَا لَكَ أَزْوَاجَكَ﴾ ("Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives," 33:50). The order of revelation is not the order of the Muṣḥaf.

﴿وَلَوْ أَعْجَبَكَ﴾ (even if it pleased you) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject, which is the pronoun in tabaddala, not from the object, which is min azwāj, because that is excessively indefinite. Its sense is: "with your admiration for them being presupposed." It is also said: she was Asmāʾ bint ʿUmays al-Khathʿamiyyah, wife of Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib, and the meaning is that she was among those whose beauty pleased him. He excepted from those forbidden to him the female slaves.

﴿رَقِيبًا﴾ (watcher) means a guardian and overseer (muhaymin). It is a warning against transgressing His limits and overstepping His lawful into His unlawful.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 53:

"That it be permitted to you" is in the sense of a temporal adverb (zarf), its implied meaning being: "at the time that it is permitted to you." And "not waiting for it" (ghayra nazirina) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "do not enter." The exception applies to both the time and the state together. As if it were said: "Do not enter the houses of the Prophet ﷺ except at the time of permission, and do not enter them except without waiting for it." These were people who would watch for the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ food, so they would enter and sit waiting for it to be ready. Its meaning is:

"Do not enter, O you who watch for the food, unless you are permitted to come to a meal, not waiting for it. And were it not for these people in particular, it would not be lawful for anyone to enter the houses of the Prophet ﷺ except with a specific permission, namely permission to come to the meal and nothing more." It is reported from Ibn Abi Ablah that he read "ghayra nazirina" in the genitive, as an attribute of "ta'am" (food). This is not the correct reading, because it departs from what it properly refers to: the pronoun that belongs to what is referred to should then be made explicit in the wording, so one would say "ghayra nazirina inahu antum" (not waiting for its ripening, you), like your saying "Hind, Zayd's wife, he struck her." "Inan al-ta'am" means its ripening (idrakuhu).

It is said: "anā al-ta'am yani" (the food ripened), like your saying "qalāhu qalā" (he hated it, he hated it). From this is His saying: "between boiling water and fierce heat (bayna hamimin ani)" and "reaching its time (baligh inahu)." It is also said that inahu means its time, i.e.: not waiting for the time of the food and the hour of its eating. It is reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ held a wedding feast for Zaynab with dates, sawiq and a sheep, and he commanded Anas to invite the people. They came in successive groups: one group would eat and leave, then another group would enter, until [Anas] said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have invited people until I can find no one left to invite." He said: "Lift your food." The people dispersed, but three men remained, conversing at length. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up so that they would leave, and went to the room of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and said: "Peace be upon you, people of the house." They said: "And upon you be peace, O Messenger of Allah. How did you find your household?" He went around the rooms, greeting each of them and they supplicated for him. He returned and found the three still sitting and conversing. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was extremely shy, so he turned away. When they saw him turning away, they left. [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Anas, and it has several chains and wordings in both collections.]]

Then it was revealed: "And not lingering for conversation (wa la mustanisina li-hadith)". They were forbidden from prolonging their sitting, such that some would become familiar with one another for the sake of a discourse one of them was delivering to the others. Or they were forbidden from listening intently to the conversation of the household. Its "istis'ana" means: to listen to it and to eavesdrop upon it. It is in the genitive, coordinated with "nazirina." It is also said that it is in the accusative, meaning: "and do not enter them as those who are becoming familiar." In His saying "fa-yastahi minkum" (so He is shy of you) there must be an implied noun, i.e., "from your leaving", as evidenced by His saying "wa-Allahu la yastahi min al-haqq" (and Allah is not shy of the truth), meaning that your leaving is something of which one should not be shy. Since shyness is what restrains the shy person from certain acts, it was said "la yastahi min al-haqq" in the sense of: He does not refrain from it or abandon it, as the shy person among you abandons it. This is a courtesy with which Allah taught the burdensome guests. It is reported from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "It is enough as a rebuke to burdensome guests that Allah the Exalted did not tolerate them and said: 'But when you have eaten, disperse.'" [[Al-Tha'labi related it through al-'Ala': "I heard 'A'ishah say this." I say: this is written thus in the hand of the one who took it out, and it is a clear and very great error. For al-'Ala only narrates from Ibn 'A'ishah, author of al-Nawadir, and he did not meet the companions of the companions of 'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, let alone 'A'ishah herself. Probably the original read "Ibn 'A'ishah," and the word "Ibn" fell out.]]

It was read: "la yastahi" with a single yā'. The pronoun in "sa'altumuhunna" refers to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and they were not mentioned because the context clearly indicates them. "Matā'an" (an object): "fas'aluhunna" (ask them) for the item. It is said: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, had a very strong desire for the veiling of them to be imposed, mentioned it often, and wished that a revelation would come concerning it. He used to say: "If only they had obeyed you concerning them, no eye would have seen them." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon you; so if you ordered the Mothers of the Believers to observe the veil..." [[Agreed upon from two hadiths, this being one of them. Al-Nasa'i and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad and al-Tabarani in al-Saghir related it through Mujahid from 'A'ishah, who said: "I was eating with the Prophet ﷺ from a dish of hays. 'Umar passed by and he called him, and he ate. His finger touched my finger, and 'Umar said: 'Oh, if only they obeyed you concerning them, no eye would have seen them.' Then the veil was revealed." Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabari related it through Mujahid as a mursal report, and al-Daraqutni corrected it in al-'Ilal. The second was also related by al-Nasa'i through Anas from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon you; so if you veiled the Mothers of the Believers...' Then Allah revealed the verse of the veil." Its origin is in the Sahih.]] So the verse was revealed. It is also reported that 'Umar passed by them while they were with the women in the mosque [[Al-Tha'labi related it from the narration of Mujahid from al-Sha'bi, who said: "'Umar passed by the wives of the Prophet ﷺ," and he mentioned it]], and said: "If you veil yourselves, then indeed you have superiority over women, just as your husband has superiority over men." Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O son of al-Khattab, you are jealous of us, while revelation descends in our houses." They did not wait but a short while before the verse was revealed. It is also said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eating with some of his companions, and the hand of one of them touched the hand of 'A'ishah. The Prophet ﷺ disliked that, [[This is in the hadith of al-Nasa'i that we mentioned at the beginning.]] and so the verse of the veil was revealed.

It is mentioned that some of them said: "Are we to forbid ourselves from speaking to the daughters of our paternal uncles except from behind a veil? If Muhammad dies, I will marry 'A'ishah." So Allah informed them that this was forbidden. [[Ibn Sa'd related it from al-Waqidi, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, from Ibn Abi 'Awn, from Ibn Bakr ibn Hizam: this verse was revealed concerning Talhah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ dies, I will marry 'A'ishah." 'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar informed us from Qatadah that a man said: "If Muhammad dies, I will surely marry 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her," so Allah the Exalted revealed: "And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah..." (the verse). Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related through Dawud from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, that he said: "It was revealed concerning a man who intended to marry some of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ," (the hadith). Through al-Suddi: the one who resolved upon that was 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]] "And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah, nor to marry his wives after him." Their marrying after him is described as something grave in His sight, and it is one of the signs of Allah's exaltation of His Messenger and the obligation of honoring him, alive and dead. Informing him of this is something that gladdens his soul, delights his heart, and draws out his gratitude, for such thoughts occur to a man and his mind is not free of them. Among people there are some whose jealousy for the sanctity of their wives is so excessive that they wish death upon them, lest they be married after them. It is related of one of the young men that he had a slave-girl for whom he had such passionate attachment and infatuation [[His saying "for whom he had no regard for the world except in her, passion and infatuation": in al-Sihah: "So-and-so is infatuated with wine," i.e., devoted to it, not caring what is said about him. (A'ii)]] that one day he looked at her, sighed deeply, and wept, and his weeping was such that his thoughts took him in this direction. He continued in this state until he killed her, imagining what might happen after his death if she remained and fell into the hand of another. It is related from some jurists that the second husband in the case of the triple divorce is a kind of punishment, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was protected from anything that would evoke that.

If you disclose anything, whether you speak of it openly or conceal it in your hearts, [then know that] indeed Allah has knowledge of it and will call you to account for it. He mentioned it immediately after this in a general form, covering everything that is shown or hidden, so that it would include their marriage (to the Prophet) and other matters. And because this manner of expression is more awe-inspiring and more weighty.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verse 55:

It is related that when the verse of hijab was revealed, the fathers, the sons and the relatives said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we also speak to them from behind the hijab?" So the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon them﴾, meaning there is no sin upon them in not veiling themselves from these people. He did not mention the paternal uncle (ʿamm) and the maternal uncle (khāl), because they take the place of the parents, and the paternal uncle has indeed been called "father" (ab).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾, and Ishmael was the paternal uncle of Jacob.

It was also said that leaving off veiling before them was disliked, because they describe the women to their sons, and their sons are not mahram. Then the speech shifts from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khitab), and in this shift there is something that indicates the excellence of the emphasis. So it was said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in what you have been commanded regarding the veil, and what revelation has sent down concerning concealment; and be lenient in it and in what has been excepted from it, to the extent you are able. Guard their limits and follow the path of piety in guarding them, and let your conduct in veiling be better than it was when you were unveiled, so that your secret may excel your public. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾, of the secret and the public, and the outward and inward of the veil, [He] whose knowledge of circumstances is never unequal.

Recited as *wa-malā'ikatuhu* with the *raf'* (nominative) ending, as a coordination with the position (*maḥall*) of *inna* and its subject (*wa-malā'ikatuhu*: "and His angels"). This is apparent according to the school of the Kufans, while the Basrans have their own explanation of it. The predicate may be omitted, since it is indicated by *yuṣallūna 'alayhi* (﴿they send blessings upon him﴾), and the sense is: ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾, that is, say: "The blessing upon the Messenger and peace." Its meaning is supplication that Allah show mercy to him and grant him peace.

If you ask: Is sending blessings upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) obligatory or recommended? I say: Rather, it is obligatory, though the scholars differ regarding the circumstances of its obligation. Some made it obligatory whenever his name is mentioned. There is a hadith: "Whoever is mentioned in his presence and does not send blessings upon me, and then enters the Fire, may Allah distance him."[[Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted it through Muḥammad ibn 'Umar, from Abū Salamah, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) ascended the pulpit and said: "Āmīn, āmīn, āmīn." He said: "Jibrīl came to me and mentioned the hadith," and in it: "Whoever is mentioned in your presence and does not send blessings upon you, and dies and enters the Fire, may Allah distance him." On this topic there are also reports from Mālik ibn al-Ḥuwayrith in Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ṭabarānī, from Ibn 'Abbās in al-Ṭabarānī, likewise from Jābir ibn Samurah, 'Abdullāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jaz' al-Zubaydī, from Buraydah in Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, from 'Ammār ibn Yāsir in al-Bazzār, and from Jābir ibn 'Abdullāh in al-Bayhaqī's Shu'ab.]] It is also reported that it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about the words of Allah, ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾?" He (ﷺ) said: "This is from the hidden knowledge, and had you not asked me about it, I would not have informed you of it. Indeed, Allah has appointed two angels to watch over me. Whenever I am mentioned in the presence of a Muslim servant and he sends blessings upon me, those two angels say: 'May Allah forgive you.' And Allah, together with His angels, responds to those two angels: 'Āmīn.' And whenever I am mentioned in the presence of a Muslim servant and he does not send blessings upon me, those two angels say: 'May Allah not forgive you.' And Allah, together with His angels, says to those two angels: 'Āmīn.'"[[Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tha'labī transmitted it from the hadith of al-Ḥasan ibn 'Alī. In its chain is al-Ḥakam ibn 'Abdullāh ibn Khaṭṭāf, who is abandoned (matrūk).]] Others said: It is obligatory once in every gathering, even if the mention is repeated, as was said regarding the verse of prostration and the blessing for one who sneezes; and likewise at the beginning and end of every supplication. Others made it obligatory once in a lifetime, and likewise they said regarding the declaration of the two testimonies (shahādatayn). What is required by caution is sending blessings upon him at every mention, because of the reports that have come, [[Among them is the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: "May he be humbled, a man in whose presence I am mentioned and who does not send blessings upon me." Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted it. On this topic there is a report from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah transmitted by al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī in Shu'ab; and from Jābir in al-Bukhārī's al-Adab al-Mufrad and in al-Ṭabarānī's al-Awsaṭ; and from 'Abdullāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jaz' in Ibn Abī 'Āṣim's Kitāb Faḍl al-Ṣalāh 'alā al-Nabī (ﷺ). Among them is the hadith of 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with him): "The miser is one in whose presence I am mentioned and who does not send blessings upon me." Al-Tirmidhī transmitted it through 'Ammārah ibn Ghaziyyah, from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥusayn, from his father, from Ḥusayn ibn 'Alī, from 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with him). Al-Nasā'ī and Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted it by this route without mention of 'Alī. Al-Ḥākim transmitted it by this route and said: "from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Alī ibn al-Ḥusayn, from Abū Hurayrah." The phrase "they harm Allah and His Messenger" has two interpretations. The first is that harming them is a figurative expression (majaz, a non-literal usage) for doing what they dislike and do not approve of: disbelief and acts of disobedience, denying prophethood, opposing the Shariah, and all kinds of hurt they inflicted on the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I have made it figurative for both, and the literal sense (haqiqah) of harming applies to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that a single expression does not carry both the figurative and the literal meaning. The second interpretation is that it means they harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) literally. It has been said regarding harming Allah: it is the saying of the Jews, Christians and polytheists, "The hand of Allah is chained," "the third of three," "the Messiah is the son of Allah," "the angels are the daughters of Allah," and "the idols are His partners." It has also been said: it is the saying of those who deviate regarding His names and attributes. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related, from his Lord: "The son of Adam insults Me, and it is not fitting for him to insult Me; and he harms Me, and it is not fitting for him to harm Me. As for his insulting Me, it is his saying: 'I have taken a son.' As for his harming Me, it is his saying: 'Allah will not bring me back after He has originated me.'" And from Ikrimah: it is the deed of the makers of images who seek to create the like of Allah's creation. [[Narrated by al-Tabari from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, similar to it.]] It has been said regarding harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): their saying "sorcerer," "poet," "soothsayer," "madman." It has been said: the breaking of his incisor and the wounding of his face on the day of Uhud. It has been said: their criticism of him regarding his marriage to Safiyyah bint Huyayy. The harming of Allah and His Messenger is stated without qualification, while the harming of the believing men and women is qualified, because the harming of Allah and His Messenger is always without right.

As for harming the believing men and women, it is of one kind and another kind. The meaning of "without what they have earned" is without any offence or deserving of harm. It has been said: it was revealed concerning some hypocrites who harmed Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said it within his hearing. It has been said: it was revealed concerning those who spread the slander against Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. It has been said: it was revealed concerning fornicators who used to follow women while they were unwilling.

From al-Fudayl: it is not lawful for you to harm a dog or a pig without right, so how much more (is it unlawful to harm) the believing men and women. Ibn Awn would not rent out shops except to people of protected status (dhimmis), because of the fright they cause when the year turns around.

The *jilbab* (a wide outer garment, wider than the *khimar* and less than a *rida'*) is what a woman wraps around her head, leaving a part of it hanging down over her chest. Ibn 'Abbas radiya Allahu 'anhuma said: it is the *rida'* that covers from above to below.

It was also said: it is the *mulhafa* (a wrapper) and anything one covers oneself with, whether a blanket or other cloth. Abu Zubayd said:

*"Welcome to a guest, whenever he asks for the door to be opened, / clad in the blackness of night as a jilbab."*

This is by Abu Zubayd. *Ahlan* is an object of a verb omitted obligatorily, meaning: "You have come to a family." *Bi-dayf* is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "I welcome a guest." It is also permissible for it to be connected to *ahlan*, since it carries the sense of welcome. *Ma* is a verbal (temporal) particle, meaning: "for the duration of the door's being opened." What is intended is generalization, meaning: at whatever time he asks for the door to be opened. He described him as coming in the blackness of night, exaggerating in praise of generosity. It is also permissible that the guest is his beloved, in which case the night is ??? *istazallaha* (?). He compared the concealment of his guest to the darkness of night, which wears a garment, and the figurative usage in *al-jalbaba* or *al-jilbab* is by way of the explicit metaphor. It is also permissible for *ma* to be a negation, and on this basis it is valid for the address to be to the Angel of Death, since he entered without asking for the door to be opened, although the guest and the beloved may also do that.

The meaning of ﴿يُدْنِينَ عَلَيْهِنَّ مِنْ جَلَابِيبِهِنَّ﴾ is: they let their outer garments down over themselves, and cover their faces and their sides with them. It is said: when the cloth slips from a woman's face, one says: "Draw your garment over your face."

That is because at the beginning of Islam, women were, as in the *jahiliyya* (the pre-Islamic period), in their habitual state of ordinary dress: a woman would go out in a shift (*dir'*) and a head-covering (*khimar*), and this distinguished the free woman from the slave woman. Young men and the roguish would, when the women went out at night to attend to their needs in the palm groves and the orchards, accost the slave women, and sometimes they would accost free women under the pretext of their being slaves, saying: "We thought she was a slave." So they were commanded to differ in their dress from the dress of slave women, by wearing outer robes (*ardiya*) and wrappers (*malahif*) and covering their heads and faces, so that they would be modest and dignified, and no one who desires them would covet them. That is the meaning of His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ أَدْنَىٰ أَنْ يُعْرَفْنَ﴾, that is: more fitting and more appropriate that they be recognized, so that they will not be accosted and will not encounter what they dislike.

If you ask: what is the meaning of *min* in ﴿مِنْ جَلَابِيبِهِنَّ﴾? I say: it is partitive (*lil-tab'id*). However, the partitive meaning admits two interpretations. The first: that they wrap themselves in some of their outer garments, meaning that the free woman should not be in ordinary dress of shift and head-covering like the slave woman and the servant, and that she should have two outer garments or more in her house.

The second: that the woman lets down part of her outer garment and lets it fall over her face, veiling herself so that she is distinguished from the slave woman. It is reported from Ibn Sirin: I asked 'Ubayda al-Salmani about this, and he said: that she puts her cloak above her eyebrow, then turns it around until she places it over her nose. It is reported from al-Suddi: that she covers one of her eyes and her forehead, and the other side except the eye.

It is reported from al-Kisa'i: they veil themselves with their wrappers drawn tightly around them, by "tightening" meaning the sense of letting down.

﴿وَكَانَ اللَّهُ غَفُورًا﴾ for what has passed of their negligence, together with repentance. [[His saying "for what has passed of their negligence together with repentance" is the view of the Mu'tazila (a theological school). Or by mere bounty according to Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna). (ع)]], because this is something that can be known by reason.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 33, verses 60–62:

﴿Those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ are a people among whom there was weakness of faith and little steadfastness in it. It is also said: they are the fornicators and the immoral, from His saying, ﴿so that he in whose heart is a disease should feel desire﴾.

﴿And those who spread false rumours﴾ are people who used to spread bad news about the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: "They were defeated and killed, and such-and-such happened to them," thereby breaking the hearts of the believers. It is said: "arjafa bikadha" means that he reported such a thing without its being true, because it was an unstable, unsettled report, from ar-rajfah, which is tremor (al-zalzalah). The meaning is: If the hypocrites do not desist from their enmity and their plotting against you, and the sinners from their immorality, and those who spread rumours from what they fabricate of bad news:

we will certainly set you against them, to do to them the deeds that displease and burden them [[His words "al-afa'il allati tasuwuhum wa tanu'uhum" (the deeds that displease them and burden them). In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) it is said: "He has against me what sa'ahu and na'ahu," meaning, what weighed him down. Some of them said: he meant sa'ahu and na'ahu, and he said na'ahu, which is not transitive, for the sake of sa'ahu, so that the speech would rhyme (yazdawij).]], then to compel them to seek exile from the city, and that they will not dwell with you in it except for a little time, just long enough to depart and gather up themselves and their dependants [[Mahmud said: "The intended meaning of His words ﴿except for a little﴾ is only the time to gather their dependants and themselves." Ahmad said: In it there is an indication that whoever is ordered to vacate a dwelling owned by another, on a lawful basis, should be given a respite, perhaps [? ] to move with himself, his goods and his dependants for a period of time, until he obtains another dwelling according to his effort (ijtihad). And Allah knows best.]]. This is called "ighra'" (incitement), which is metaphorically "tahrish" (stirring up).

﴿Cursed﴾: it is in the accusative either as an object of reviling or as a circumstantial state (hal). That is: they will not dwell with you except as cursed. The particle of exception has entered upon both the adverbial expression of time and the state together, as was explained in His words ﴿unless permission is given to you for a meal, not waiting for its preparation﴾ (33:53). It cannot be governed by "uhidhu" (they were seized), because what follows the conditional particle does not govern what comes before it.

It is also said that "qalilan" is likewise in the accusative as a state. Its meaning: they will not dwell with you except as few, humbled, and cursed.

If you ask: What is the place of ﴿they will not dwell with you﴾? I answer: It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "la-nughriyannaka" (we will certainly set you against them), because it is permissible for the oath to be answered by it. Do you not see the soundness of your saying: "If they do not desist, they will not dwell with you"?

If you ask: Should it not have been right for ﴿they will not dwell with you﴾ to be coordinated with fa' (so), and for it to say: "We will set you against them, so they will not dwell with you"? I answer: If the second had been made a consequence (musabbab) of the first, the matter would be as you say. But it was made a separate answer to the oath, coordinated with the first. It was coordinated with thumma (then) because exile from homelands was greater for them and greater than everything else with which they were afflicted, so its state was delayed from the state of what it was coordinated with.

﴿The sunnah of Allah﴾ is in the place of an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad), meaning: Allah has established a way (sunnah) concerning those who oppose the prophets, that they be killed wherever they are found. It is related from Muqatil: that is, as the people of Badr were killed and taken captive.

Al-Sa'ir: the blazing fire, intensely kindled.
Al-Sa'ir: the blazing fire, intensely kindled.

Recited also as "tuqallabu" (in the passive form), and "tuqallabu" meaning "tataqallabu" (fluctuates/turns about), and "nuqallibu" meaning "we turn them about."

[Note on "tuqallabu" as governed by the Fire: that is, "their faces" in the accusative case (a note by the editor: "(ʿ)").] The meaning of turning them about is causing them to move in all directions, as you see a piece of meat turning in a pot when it boils, the bubbling tossing it from one side to the other. Or it means changing them from their states and transforming them from their forms. Or it means casting them into the Fire face down and upside down. The faces are singled out for mention because the face is the most honoured part of a human being's body. It is also permissible for "the face" to stand for the whole person, with the adverbial "on the day" governed by "yaqulūna" or by a verb omitted, namely "remember." If the adverb is governed by the omitted verb, then "yaqulūna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Also read: "sādatanā" and "sādātanā" (our masters and our leaders), meaning the heads of disbelief who taught them disbelief and made it attractive to them. It is said: "ḍalla al-sabīl" and "aḍallahu iyyāh" (he went astray from the way, and he caused him to go astray from it). The lengthening alif [in "al-sabīlā" and "al-rasūlā"] is for the sake of prolonging the voice: the verse-endings (fawāṣil al-āy) were made like the rhyme-endings (qawāfī) of poetry. Its benefit is pausing and indicating that the speech has ended and what follows is a new statement.

Also read: "kathīran" (much), intensifying the number of the curses; and "kabīran" (great), to indicate the most severe and greatest curse. "Ḍi'fayn" (doubled): double for his own misguidance and double for his misguiding others. [They will] acknowledge, plead for help, and wish, but none of that will benefit them.

The Trust here means obedience, because it is necessarily bound to existence, just as the trust (amanah) is necessarily bound to being discharged. Its being offered to the inanimate things, their refusal, and their fear are metaphorical.

As for "carrying the Trust" (haml al-amanah), it is from your saying: "So-and-so is a bearer of the trust and one who takes it upon himself," meaning that he does not deliver it to its owner until it leaves his charge and he is released from its obligation, because the trust is as if it rides the one entrusted with it, while he is its carrier. Do you not see them saying: "Debts mounted him" (rakibathu al-duyun), and "he has a right over him" (wali 'alayhi haqq)? When he discharges it, it no longer rides him, nor is he its carrier. Similar to this is their saying: "a client (mawla) does not possess victory for another client," meaning that he gives support to him and is lenient with it, and does not withhold it as the one who forsakes withholds. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Your brother is the one whose self you do not possess in compassion,
and who scatters at the angry things (al-muhfizat al-katai'f)."

[[By al-Qutami. It is also said: for Dhu al-Rummah. Hassa lahu hassan: he felt tender towards him and was kind. Al-hass also means intellect, planning, and considering consequences; al-irfidad means scattering and dispersal, and ahfazahu ihfazan: he angered him, so al-muhfizat: the things that anger. Al-katai'f: plural of katifa, which is rancor and enmity. He says: your brother is the one whose self does not possess mercy, but gives it to you. Or his self is not able to deliberate calmly, but he hastens to you suddenly and trembles, and his rancors toward you vanish in matters that anger you, because they also anger him.]]

That is, he does not withhold tenderness and kindness as the miserly owner holds what is in his hand, but gives it and allows it. From this is their saying: "Abghidu haqqa akhika?" (Do you hate your brother's right?), because if he loves him he does not bring it out to his brother nor discharge it, and if he hates him he brings it out and discharges it. So the meaning of "fa-abayna an yahmilnaha wa-hamalaha al-insan" (they refused to bear it, and man bore it) is: they refused except to discharge it, and man refused except to be a bearer of it who does not discharge it. Then He described him as wrongdoing (zalum) because he abandons the discharge of the trust, and as ignorant (jahul) because he errs in what would make him happy while he is able to do it, namely discharging it. The second view: what man was charged with is so great and heavy in its burden that it was offered to the greatest and strongest and most powerful of the bodies God created, to bear it and be independent in it, and they refused to carry it and feared it, while man bore it despite his weakness and the slackness of his strength, "Indeed he was wrongdoing, ignorant," since he carried the trust and then did not fulfill it, and undertook it and then broke his guarantee regarding it. Similar to this in Arabic speech is much. The Qur'an came only in accordance with their methods and styles in such matters. Among them is their saying: "If it were said to fat: where are you going?" it would say: "to straighten the crookedness." And for them there are many proverbs on the tongues of animals and inanimate things. The conversation of fat is impossible, but the purpose is that fatness in an animal is something that makes its ugliness beautiful, just as leanness is something that makes its beauty ugly. So it depicted the effect of fatness in it in a way that falls more heavily on the hearer's soul, makes him more at ease with it and more receptive to it, and more firmly fixed upon its reality. Likewise the depiction of the greatness of the Trust, the difficulty of its matter, the weight of its burden, and fulfilling it.

If you say: the aspect of the figurative comparison is known in their saying to one who does not hold to one opinion: "I see you advancing one foot and delaying the other," because his state is likened, in his swaying and tilting between two opinions and his leaving off proceeding on either, to the state of one who hesitates in his going and does not gather his feet for proceeding in his direction. Each of the figure and the figured is something sound, falling under correctness and knowledge. That is not so in this verse, for the offering of the Trust to the inanimate and their refusal and fear is impossible in itself and not sound, so how is the construction of the figure upon the impossible valid? Its example is only that you liken something to what is not conceivable. I say: the thing used as the comparison in the verse, and in their saying "If it were said to fat: where are you going?", and in its like, is supposed, and suppositions are imagined in the mind just as realities are. The state of the obligation in its difficulty and the weight of its burden is likened to its supposed state, if it were offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, they would refuse to bear it and fear it. The lam in "liyu'adhdhiba" (so that He may punish) is the lam of causation by way of metaphor, because punishment is the result of bearing the trust, just as discipline in "he struck him for discipline" is the result of striking. Al-A'mash read "wa-yatuba" (and He relents) so that the cause is restricted to the act of the bearer, and it begins: "wa-yatubu Allah" (and God relents) [[His saying "wa-yatubu", i.e. with raf', as in al-Nasafi. (Ibn Abbad)]]. The meaning of the common reading: that God punishes the bearer of the trust and relents toward others who did not bear it, because when one who fulfills is forgiven, that is a kind of punishment for the treacherous. And God knows best.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Ahzab and teaches it to his family and those whom his right hand possesses, will be granted security from the punishment of the grave."
